marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q016.takeaway: The ovaries are not contents of the broad ligament; the mesovarium connects the ovarian hilum to its posterior surface.
marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q016.displayText:
The ovaries are not contents of the broad ligament; the mesovarium connects the ovarian hilum to its posterior surface.

The ovaries are not the contents of the broad ligament.

Ovaries are suspended in the pelvic cavity by the mesovarium. It attaches only the hilum of the

ovary to the posterior surface of the broad ligament. The majority of the ovarian surface is covered

by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium which imparts a dull white color to the ovaries.
emphasis: The ovaries are not contents of the broad ligament; the mesovarium connects the ovarian hilum to its posterior surface

rationales.a: The round ligament runs through the broad ligament region from the uterus toward the inguinal canal and is not the excluded structure.
rationales.b: The uterine tube lies in the superior margin of the broad ligament (mesosalpinx).
rationales.c: Broad-ligament connective tissue can contain vessels and lymphatics; the ovary is attached by mesovarium rather than enclosed as a content.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q017.takeaway: The proper ovarian ligament connects the inferomedial ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus.
marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q017.displayText:
The proper ovarian ligament connects the inferomedial ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus.

The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) attaches the inferomedial extremity of the ovary to

the lateral angle of the uterus.

Other ligamentous supports of the ovaries:

+ Infundibulo pelvic ligament (suspensory ligament) - attaches the lateral surface of the ovary to the peritoneum lining the lateral pelvic wall. It contains the ovarian vessels and nerves. + Mesovarium - a short peritoneal fold that attaches the ovary to the back of the broad ligament. This carries blood vessels and nerves to the hilum of the ovary. marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q018.takeaway: Ovarian lymphatics follow the ovarian vessels to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near their aortic origin.
marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q018.displayText:
Ovarian lymphatics follow the ovarian vessels to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near their aortic origin.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of serous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary. It spreads to the para-aortic nodes because the ovary drains alongside the origin of the ovarian arteries. The source table summarizes lymphatic drainage of the vulva, vagina, cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries.
emphasis: Ovarian lymphatics follow the ovarian vessels to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near their aortic origin

rationales.a: External iliac nodes drain some pelvic structures but are not the primary route for ovarian lymph, which follows ovarian vessels upward.
rationales.b: Internal iliac nodes receive lymph from many pelvic viscera but are not the principal ovarian drainage group.
rationales.c: Obturator nodes are part of pelvic drainage and do not receive the main lymphatic route from the ovary.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q019.takeaway: The uterine tube is lined by simple ciliated columnar epithelium, resembling bronchiolar epithelium.
marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q019.displayText:
The uterine tube is lined by simple ciliated columnar epithelium, resembling bronchiolar epithelium.

The lining epithelium of the fallopian tube is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium. It is similar to the epithelium of the bronchioles.

The ciliated epithelial cells are predominant in the distal part of the fallopian tube. There is an increase in the height and number of cilia during the estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle.

Other cells include secretory or peg cells, maximally located in the proximal portion of the tube; these are active around ovulation and their secretions help in capacitation of sperms. Intraepithelial lymphocytes may occasionally be present.

Option A: stomach epithelium is simple columnar. Option B: tracheal epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar. Option D: proximal convoluted tubule epithelium is cuboidal with microvilli.
emphasis: The uterine tube is lined by simple ciliated columnar epithelium, resembling bronchiolar epithelium

rationales.a: The stomach is lined mainly by simple columnar mucus-secreting cells, not the ciliated epithelium of the uterine tube.
rationales.b: Tracheal epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells rather than simple ciliated columnar epithelium.
rationales.d: Proximal convoluted tubule epithelium is simple cuboidal with a brush border, not ciliated columnar.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q020.takeaway: The cardinal (transverse cervical/Mackenrodt) ligament extends from cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic wall.
marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q020.displayText:
The cardinal (transverse cervical/Mackenrodt) ligament extends from cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic wall.

The cardinal ligament (transverse cervical ligament or ligament of Mackenrodt) extends from the side of the cervix and lateral fornix of the vagina to the pelvic wall. Other ligaments of the uterus: + Broad ligament - peritoneal fold covering the ovaries and fallopian tubes. It has three parts named after the structures it covers, i.e., mesosalpinx, mesovarium, and mesometrium (largest part). + Pubocervical ligament - attaches the anterior aspect of the cervix and upper vagina to the posterior aspect of the pubic bones. + Round ligaments - arises from the lateral cornua of the uterus, passes through the inguinal canal, and attaches to the labia majora. @ + Uterosacral ligaments - passes from the back of the uterus and cervix to thegintérior surface of the sacrum. emphasis: The cardinal (transverse cervical/Mackenrodt) ligament extends from cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic wall

rationales.a: The broad ligament is a peritoneal sheet associated with uterus, tubes and ovaries; it is not the principal cervix-to-wall support described.
rationales.b: The pubocervical ligament runs anteriorly from cervix/upper vagina toward pubis, not laterally to the pelvic wall.
rationales.c: The round ligament extends from the uterine horn through the inguinal canal, not from cervix/vagina to lateral wall.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q021.takeaway: Waldeyer's (presacral) fascia is posterior to the rectum, not a direct posterior relation of the vagina.
marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q021.displayText:
Waldeyer's (presacral) fascia is posterior to the rectum, not a direct posterior relation of the vagina.

Waldeyer's fascia (presacral fascia) forms a posterior relationship of the rectum and is not related to the vagina. It lines the anterior surface of the sacrum. The source table and diagrams describe anterior, posterior, and lateral relations of the vagina.
emphasis: Waldeyer's (presacral) fascia is posterior to the rectum, not a direct posterior relation of the vagina

rationales.a: The rectovaginal septum separates vagina from rectum and is a posterior vaginal relation.
rationales.b: The rectouterine pouch lies posterior to the uterus and upper vagina and is among the posterior relations listed.
rationales.d: The perineal body supports the posterior distal vagina and is a recognized relation.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q022.takeaway: The internal iliac system supplies the vagina, including paired longitudinal azygos vaginal arteries on its anterior and posterior walls.
marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q022.displayText:
The internal iliac system supplies the vagina, including paired longitudinal azygos vaginal arteries on its anterior and posterior walls.

The internal iliac artery gives rise to the azygous arteries of the vagina. These are longitudinal median vessels on the anterior and posterior surfaces of the vagina. The vagina also receives blood supply from uterine, internal pudendal, and middle rectal branches of the internal iliac artery. The source table summarizes arterial supply and venous drainage of the vulva, clitoris, vagina, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries.
emphasis: The internal iliac system supplies the vagina, including paired longitudinal azygos vaginal arteries on its anterior and posterior walls

rationales.b: The obturator artery supplies the medial thigh and pelvic wall; it is not the source of the vaginal azygos arteries.
rationales.c: The external iliac artery continues to the lower limb and does not give rise to the vaginal azygos vessels.
rationales.d: The median sacral artery is a small midline posterior vessel and is not the source identified for vaginal arterial supply.
